lane.name: Countrygaze and loud twang
lane.definition: Shoegaze- and noise-rock-scale guitar walls under pedal steel, twang, and country-song structures; the Wednesday template.

albums.album: How Do You Let Love Into the Heart That Isn't Split Wide Open
albums.label: Sub-Fi
albums.description: An early, quietly-released Wednesday EP from just after the band's formation, rawer and more hushed than anything on their later Dead Oceans records.
albums.lineage: Part of the pre-Lenderman early catalog that shows the band's sound before its shoegaze/noise elements arrived.
key_tracks: How Do You Let Love Into the Heart That Isn't Split Wide Open

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Wednesday's self-released debut: hazy, unpolished indie rock recorded long before the band's louder albums. It already leans on Karly Hartzman's diaristic, Southern-gothic lyrics, sung plainly over rough, lo-fi guitars.
albums.lineage: The starting point of Hartzman's project, years before the shoegaze/country fusion of Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God.

albums.label: Manic Static
albums.description: A self-titled EP from the band's early period, cheaply recorded and rough around the edges. It points toward the heavier guitar textures of the albums to come, with Hartzman's plainspoken vocals up front.
albums.lineage: Bridges yep definitely and the fuller-band sound of I Was Trying to Describe You to Someone.

albums.album: I Was Trying to Describe You to Someone
albums.label: Orindal Records
albums.description: Wednesday's first proper album and first for Orindal: thick, shoegaze-leaning guitars wrapped around Hartzman's vivid, small-town storytelling. It is quieter than Rat Saw God but has the same eye for uncomfortable detail.
albums.lineage: First album to show the full band's mix of noise rock and alt-country, setting up Twin Plagues.

albums.label: Acrobat Unstable Records
albums.description: Fuzzed-out, noisy indie rock that sits near countrygaze without being built around it. 'Kerrytown' is the clearest crossover point, its Americana tinge recalling Wilco and Silver Jews inside a record otherwise driven by distortion.
albums.lineage: Sounds akin to Wednesday-adjacent noise/twang bands, though it arrived alongside rather than after them.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A debut of loose demos that set Dutch Interior's template: scuzzy tape hiss, wandering slide-ish guitar leads, and a slack, almost countrified drawl buried under distortion. Rougher and stranger than the records that followed, it plays like a sketchbook for the noisy-Americana sound they'd refine on Moneyball.
albums.lineage: Grew out of the LA DIY scene alongside bands trading Crazy Horse fuzz for twang; feeds directly into Blinded by Fame and Moneyball.
key_tracks: Three Trips to the Store, One Drunk Yukon

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Will Anderson's debut full-length as Hotline TNT buries plainspoken pop melodies under thick sheets of guitar fuzz and noise, setting up the countrygaze-adjacent wall-of-sound style he'd refine on Cartwheel. It's rawer and murkier than the later records but already has the hooks. It's for fans who want the noisiest end of the jangle/shoegaze crossover.
albums.lineage: Kicks off Hotline TNT's run from DIY noise-pop toward the more country-tinged, festival-ready sound of Cartwheel and Raspberry Moon.

albums.label: Super Enema
albums.description: A short, sparsely produced EP from the band's early period. It is rough and home-recorded, with Hartzman's plainspoken voice over loose guitars.
albums.lineage: Sounds like a transitional sketch between the band's first two albums.

albums.label: Orindal Records
albums.description: The album where Wednesday's mix of shoegaze fuzz and country twang really locked in. Loud, blown-out guitars and pedal steel sit under Hartzman's plainspoken lyrics about small-town Southern life, with songs like 'Cliff' swinging between hush and roar.
albums.lineage: Sounds indebted to Velvet Underground-descended noise textures grafted onto Southern storytelling in the Skynyrd-to-Drive-By-Truckers line.

albums.label: Audiotree
albums.description: A radio-session live album cut around the Twin Plagues era, rougher and noisier in the room than the studio versions, capturing the band's live intensity before they broke through more widely.
albums.lineage: A snapshot of the band mid-transition from lo-fi project to full-throated noise-country outfit.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: A road-trip-ready tour tape from an Inland Empire band splitting the difference between fuzz-caked shoegaze riffs and a plainspoken country vocal delivery. It is short, hazy and rough, a sketch of the sound they would build on.
albums.lineage: Sounds close to the countrygaze Bandcamp scene around Wednesday; precedes There You Ain't.

albums.album: Mowing the Leaves Instead of Piling 'em Up
albums.label: Orindal Records
albums.description: A full-band covers record pulling from country, indie and classic-rock sources, filtered through Wednesday's blown-out, pedal-steel-laced sound. It's a covers set rather than original songs, released just before the band left Orindal for Dead Oceans.
albums.lineage: Shows the covers/tribute strand of the countrygaze scene and the band's own influences in plain sight.
key_tracks: Mowing the Leaves Instead of Piling 'em Up

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: Thicker and more purposeful than the debut, this set pairs a ratty, bubblegum drum feel with whiny, screaming lead guitar and a cathartic, a-rhythmic sense of collapse. It blends country, folk and grunge, which is the whole Dutch Interior pitch in a sentence.
albums.lineage: Bridges Dutch Interior's tape-hiss beginnings and their Fat Possum signing; sounds like the Wednesday-style countrygaze template with a heavier '90s alt-rock skew.

albums.label: Really Rad Records
albums.description: A short follow-up EP built around small, specific images (a fruit arrangement, a golf dream about Willie Nelson) delivered through thick, honeyed distortion. Its sound splits the difference between Dinosaur Jr.-scale guitars and an unmistakably country vocal cadence.
albums.lineage: Extends the sound introduced on 2022 Tour Tape; sounds close to Wednesday's countrygaze.

albums.label: Self-released
albums.description: This home-recorded set mixes shoegaze walls of guitar with Primal Scream-style melodic touches and loose, woozy energy. It sits at the loud, twangy edge of countrygaze rather than its center, for listeners who like their noise-pop hazy and homespun.
albums.lineage: An off-kilter entry in the countrygaze lineage, closer to noise-pop than to Wednesday's overt country phrasing, but sharing its shoegaze-scale guitar walls.

albums.label: Rite Field Records
albums.description: Shallowater's debut earns the 'dirtgaze' tag: dusty, string-bent guitar figures get swallowed by walls of overdriven noise, with a drawled, half-buried vocal riding on top. It is rougher and more shoegaze-indebted than the band's later work, closer to noise rock with a country skeleton than to polished Americana.
albums.lineage: Debut full-length that establishes the dirtgaze sound Shallowater expand on with God's Gonna Give You A Million Dollars; part of the small post-Wednesday wave of Texas and Southern bands mixing noise-rock scale with country phrasing.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: Wednesday's breakthrough: a widescreen mix of Dinosaur Jr.-style guitar theatrics and vivid, novelistic Southern storytelling, from car crashes to church parking lots. 'Bull Believer' is the album's noisiest, most cathartic centerpiece.
albums.lineage: Sounds like the Skynyrd-to-Drive-By-Truckers storytelling line fused with Sonic Youth/Dinosaur Jr.-style guitar noise; a defining Core record for this atlas.

albums.label: Fat Possum
albums.description: Dutch Interior's Fat Possum debut pushes the noisy-twang formula into a more cohesive, full-band record without losing the ragged edges. Its golden-hour twang swings between sunny and haunting, the clearest statement yet of the band's noise-wall-over-country-changes sound.
albums.lineage: Third album for a band who came up recording to tape; sounds of a piece with Wednesday and Shallowater in the 2020s countrygaze scene.

albums.album: God's Gonna Give You A Million Dollars
albums.label: Sans Soleil Records
albums.description: Long songs, several stretching well past the usual length, swing between ear-splitting guitar walls and glacial, delicate melodies. It is the fullest realization yet of the band's dirtgaze idea: country-song bones dressed in noise-rock scale.
albums.lineage: Second Shallowater LP, expanding the noise/twang balance of There Is A Well into longer, more patient song structures; sounds of a piece with Dutch Interior and Wednesday.

albums.label: Dead Oceans
albums.description: Wednesday's latest album pushes further into explosive shoegaze and grunge territory while keeping classic country song structures underneath. Songs like 'Elderberry Wine' show the quieter, twangier side, while the loud tracks bury Hartzman's storytelling under huge guitars.
albums.lineage: Continues the countrygaze sound of the band's own Twin Plagues and Rat Saw God, now bigger and more anthemic.

albums.album: Say a Prayer to the Gods of Getting Going
albums.label: Polyvinyl
albums.description: Ella Williams' enveloping voice sits against crunchy, wall-of-guitar production on this Squirrel Flower record. Big, distorted guitars swell under slow, open melodies, giving the songs a live, room-filling weight. It suits listeners who like loud guitars wrapped around intimate songwriting.
albums.lineage: Continues Squirrel Flower's move toward the countrygaze-adjacent, guitar-wall sound of Wednesday's circle.
